text: Chapter 2 covered writing IAM policies scoped to specific S3 buckets and Glue resources — real, resource-level ARNs, not a wildcard. But IAM has a real ceiling: it can grant or deny access to a whole S3 object or Glue table, never to one column inside it. Once a role can read a table, it can read every column and every row that table's files contain.

Lake Formation supports two configurations. The default, called Open, grants the Super permission to all current IAM principals — Lake Formation's own fine-grained controls are effectively bypassed, and IAM alone decides what's visible. AWS's recommended method flips that: IAM permissions stay broad, and Lake Formation's own grants are what actually decide which tables, columns, and rows a principal can see. If a column-level grant looks like it should be restricting access but isn't, the Open method is the first thing worth checking.

This is what granting fine-grained access actually looks like: choose an IAM principal, then choose the specific Catalog permissions to grant — Create database, Select, Describe, and so on — rather than an all-or-nothing table grant.

And this is the grain IAM alone can't express — Select, Insert, Delete, Describe, Alter, and Drop, checked independently at the database level and again at the table and column level. A role can have broad access to query a table while still never being able to see one sensitive column its job doesn't require.

Naming every table and column explicitly in every grant doesn't scale. LF-Tags fix that: tag a column once with a key like sensitivity, then grant a principal access based on the tag, not the resource name. Within one tag key, values are OR'd together; across different tag keys, conditions are AND'd. The real payoff: a table created next month, tagged the same way, is covered immediately — no new grant to write.

IAM answers whether a principal can call an API at all. Lake Formation answers exactly which rows and columns a query can actually return — the same least-privilege discipline from Chapter 2, extended one level deeper. Next lesson: checking that the data itself is actually trustworthy, with AWS Glue Data Quality.
